subsection: 4. Domestic factors in US foreign policy: McCarthyism, the anti-war movement and race relations

notes.h: Cold War background and key terms for domestic politics
notes.b: US foreign policy was not made in a vacuum: presidents had to carry voters, Congress and the press with them. After 1945, fear of communism abroad turned into fear of subversion (secret undermining of the government from within) at home, and later protest and racial injustice put pressure on policy too.
points: Fear of subversion grew out of Cold War events: the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 (a pledge to resist communist expansion, called containment) and the Soviet atomic test of August 1949.
The communist victory in China (People's Republic proclaimed 1 October 1949) and the Korean War (from 25 June 1950) added to the fear, so Americans began to suspect spies and traitors at home.

Congressional committees could summon witnesses and demand answers. The Fifth Amendment of the Constitution allowed a witness to refuse to answer questions that might incriminate them. The Senate and the House of Representatives are separate chambers, each running its own investigations.

Segregation in the South, known as Jim Crow, was a system of laws keeping Black and white Americans apart in schools, transport and public places. Black Americans were fighting it in the Black freedom struggle, and the Vietnam War escalated under President Johnson from 1965.

Public opinion means what ordinary Americans thought, as measured by polls and the press. It set limits on what a president could do abroad, because a policy that voters rejected cost votes and support in Congress.

Mass media means newspapers, radio and above all television. Television carried McCarthy, the Vietnam War and the civil rights struggle into homes across the country, so that millions saw events at the same moment.

Liberalism, in US usage, means support for civil liberties (such as free speech), civil rights and an active federal government. McCarthyism attacked it, while civil rights and anti-war campaigners defended it.
McCarthyism means reckless accusation of communist subversion, made without proof. The Red Scare is the wider wave of fear of communists that began before McCarthy and outlasted him.
notes.tip: Exams use public opinion, mass media and liberalism as the ideas that link this topic. When you use one, say how it limited or shaped a decision, not only what it means.

notes.h: The Red Scare before McCarthy: loyalty tests and Hollywood
notes.b: The panic about communists did not start with Joseph McCarthy. By 1947 the government and Congress had already set up machinery to hunt for disloyal people, and Hollywood was an early target.
points: Truman's loyalty programme (Executive Order 9835, March 1947) set up loyalty review boards to investigate federal employees, and the Attorney General kept a list of 'subversive' organisations. Many federal employees feared losing their jobs over any past political association.

The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) held hearings on communist influence in Hollywood in October 1947. The Hollywood Ten, writers and directors including Dalton Trumbo, refused to say whether they were communists, and Congress cited them for contempt in November 1947.

The Ten were convicted of contempt of Congress in 1948. Their appeals failed, so they served prison terms of up to a year from 1950. This mattered because it showed that refusing to answer a congressional committee could end in prison.

The studio heads, meeting at the Waldorf-Astoria hotel in New York in November 1947, issued the Waldorf Statement. They promised not to employ the Ten or anyone suspected of communism, and this created the Hollywood blacklist (a secret ban on employing named people).
The blacklist ran for about a decade, and it began to break in 1960 when Trumbo was credited for a film. This shows how long a fear of association could shut people out of their careers.

HUAC (House, from 1938, Hollywood hearings in 1947) must not be confused with McCarthy's later Senate subcommittee. McCarthy was never a member of HUAC, and his own investigations did not concern Hollywood.
notes.tip: Keep the committees apart: HUAC was a House committee and the Hollywood Ten belong to 1947, whereas McCarthy sat in the Senate. Likewise keep Truman's loyalty programme of 1947 separate from Eisenhower's security programme of 1953.

notes.h: Spies, trials and laws: Hiss, the Rosenbergs and the Red Scare in society
notes.b: Real and alleged spy cases between 1948 and 1953 convinced many Americans that traitors were at work in government. Laws and prosecutions followed, and the fear spread into everyday working life.
points: Whittaker Chambers, an ex-communist who had been a courier and later a Time editor, accused Alger Hiss, a former State Department official, before HUAC in August 1948. Chambers said Hiss was a communist who had passed documents to him; Hiss denied it.

A time-bar (a legal limit on how long after an act charges may be brought) prevented a spy charge, so Hiss was tried for perjury. The first trial in 1949 ended in a hung jury; he was convicted in January 1950 and served about three and a half years.

Richard Nixon, a California congressman on HUAC, pressed the Hiss case, and it made his national name. Historians still debate Hiss's guilt, though most think he was guilty. This is why the case became so highly publicised.

Klaus Fuchs, a German-born British physicist who had worked on the Manhattan Project (the wartime atomic bomb programme), confessed in January 1950 and was arrested in February 1950. His confession led to the Rosenbergs' ring and so strengthened fears of atomic spies.

Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were arrested in 1950 and convicted in 1951 of conspiracy to commit espionage, for passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union. They were executed at Sing Sing on 19 June 1953.

Eleven Communist Party leaders were tried in 1949 under the Smith Act (1940), and the Supreme Court upheld their convictions in Dennis v. United States (1951). The McCarran Internal Security Act of September 1950 forced Communist organisations to register, and Congress overrode Truman's veto of it.

The Red Scare reached teachers, trade unionists and entertainers. Loyalty oaths were widely required of public employees, including teachers, and many people lost jobs for refusing to name former associates, so dissent itself became dangerous.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to tell the people and cases apart: Hiss (State Department, perjury 1950), the Rosenbergs (atomic spies, executed 1953), Fuchs (British physicist) and Chambers (the accuser). Also separate the Smith Act (1940, used 1949) from the McCarran Act (1950).

notes.h: McCarthy's rise, 1950 to 1952: Wheeling, methods and early opposition
notes.b: McCarthy was a little-known senator until early 1950. He then seized on a moment when Americans were frightened, and he made accusation his political weapon.
points: On 9 February 1950, in a Lincoln Day speech to a Republican women's club at Wheeling, West Virginia, McCarthy claimed to hold a list of communists working in the State Department. The numbers he gave later varied, and the speech text is disputed.

The speech became a national sensation because of the timing: the Hiss conviction in January 1950, the arrest of Fuchs, the Soviet bomb and the fall of China had left Americans ready to believe in traitors.

The Tydings Committee, a Senate subcommittee chaired by Millard Tydings, reported in July 1950 and called the charges a fraud and a hoax. This was the committee's verdict. Tydings then lost his Maryland seat in November 1950 after a campaign in which McCarthy's allies attacked him.

McCarthy's methods were guilt by association (damning people for the company they had kept), accusations without evidence, unnamed lists, shifting numbers, bullying of witnesses and personal smears. The cartoonist Herblock (Herbert Block of the Washington Post) coined the word McCarthyism in March 1950.

In June 1950 Margaret Chase Smith, a Republican senator from Maine, delivered her Declaration of Conscience. She criticised smear tactics without naming McCarthy, showing that some in his own party were uneasy. This mattered because criticism from inside his party was harder to dismiss.

In 1951 McCarthy attacked General George Marshall, a respected wartime commander. Eisenhower, campaigning in 1952, did not defend Marshall in McCarthy's presence in Wisconsin, a sign of how much Republicans feared to cross him. This is an example of how far fear of McCarthy reached.
notes.tip: In a paragraph on McCarthy, give the Wheeling speech with its date and claim, but never a number of names: the figures varied and the text is disputed. Do not put any McCarthy line in quotation marks.

notes.h: McCarthy at his peak and his fall, 1953 to 1954
notes.b: The Republican victory of 1952 gave McCarthy an official platform, but the same publicity that built him also destroyed him once television and Senate colleagues turned on him.
points: Republicans won the presidency and Congress in 1952. From January 1953 McCarthy chaired the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, which gave him the power to summon officials and hold hearings.

In 1953 he investigated the Voice of America (the government's overseas radio service) and the State Department's overseas libraries. His aides Roy Cohn, chief counsel, and G. David Schine toured State Department libraries in Europe checking them.

On 9 March 1954 Edward R. Murrow's CBS programme See It Now used McCarthy's own speeches and film to criticise him. It was effective because viewers saw his methods in his own words. This is why it hurt him more than press criticism.

McCarthy then turned his inquiries on the army, partly over the treatment of Schine, who had been drafted. The resulting Army-McCarthy hearings, televised from 22 April to 17 June 1954, showed him to a national audience as a bully.

On 9 June 1954 Joseph Welch, the army's counsel, rebuked McCarthy for attacking a young lawyer in Welch's firm, asking 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' This became a turning point in public opinion against him.

On 2 December 1954 the Senate voted 67 to 22 to censure him, for conduct that tended to bring the Senate into dishonour, or loosely conduct unbecoming a senator. A committee, the Watkins Committee, had recommended the censure, and after the vote his influence vanished.
notes.tip: A common question is why McCarthy fell: give television (Murrow, the hearings, Welch), then the loss of Senate colleagues and of Eisenhower's support. Do not confuse Welch, the army's counsel, with Murrow the broadcaster, or Cohn with Schine.

notes.b: McCarthy was a direct participant who used the Red Scare to build a national following, and he was also shaped by the events around him. Contemporaries and historians have judged him very differently.
points: Joseph McCarthy was born on 14 November 1908 in Grand Chute, Wisconsin, studied law at Marquette University and became a circuit judge in 1939. He served in the Marines from 1942 to 1945, later calling himself 'Tail-Gunner Joe', a claim that was exaggerated.

He won the Republican primary against the incumbent Robert La Follette Jr and was elected to the Senate in 1946 (he took his seat in January 1947). He was re-elected in 1952. This is why he could claim a mandate from Wisconsin voters.

As a participant he made the Wheeling speech of February 1950 and the investigations of 1953 to 1954, chairing the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. The Red Scare existed before him, and he rode it, exploiting the Hiss conviction, the fall of China, the Soviet bomb, Fuchs and Korea.

His fall was also shaped by events. Television exposure, the Army-McCarthy hearings, the turning of Senate colleagues and Eisenhower's refusal to help him brought him down, and the term McCarthyism outlived him as a word for smear and witch-hunt.
McCarthy died on 2 May 1957, aged 48, of acute hepatitis linked to heavy drinking. His early death at 48 ended his career as well as his influence.

Contemporaries split. Many Republicans and conservatives, and much of the Catholic and Midwest public, backed him, while liberals, most of the press and many Senate colleagues denounced his methods as reckless smears.
Historians since Richard Rovere (Senator Joe McCarthy, 1959) have judged him a demagogue (a leader who stirs up fear for personal gain).

Ellen Schrecker (Many Are the Crimes, 1998) argues that McCarthyism was a wider system, including the FBI under J. Edgar Hoover, HUAC and both parties, which he exploited rather than created, so removing him did not end the Red Scare.

M. Stanton Evans (Blacklisted by History, 2007) offered a minority defence of him. The Venona decrypts (Soviet cables made public from 1995) show a number of Soviet agents in the US government, but they proved real Soviet spying without vindicating McCarthy's methods or lists.
notes.tip: Strong answers separate the Red Scare as a wider system (HUAC, the FBI, loyalty boards, both parties) from McCarthy as a person, and name a historian for each view: Rovere or Schrecker. Do not say Venona proved McCarthy right.

notes.h: Eisenhower's security programme and the administration's caution
notes.b: When the Republicans took office in 1953, the loyalty rules of Truman were replaced, not abandoned. The new president kept the anti-communist climate in place and avoided a public fight with McCarthy.
points: Eisenhower signed Executive Order 10450 in April 1953. It replaced Truman's loyalty standard with 'security risk' criteria for federal employment, so many dismissals followed.

Under the new criteria, past membership in suspect organisations could count against a person as well as proven disloyalty, which made it easy to dismiss employees on suspicion. For example, an old membership could cost someone a federal post.
Eisenhower avoided naming McCarthy in public for most of 1953 and 1954, and kept his criticism private or indirect. This public caution meant the charges spread until the Army hearings of 1954.
Richard Nixon, Eisenhower's vice president, had built his national reputation on the Hiss investigation. This made anti-communism a bipartisan position (shared by both parties) in 1950s politics.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the executive orders: 9835 (Truman, 1947, loyalty), 10450 (Eisenhower, 1953, security risk) and 9981 (Truman, 1948, desegregating the armed forces).

notes.b: The climate of suspicion changed what officials said and did about China, the Soviet Union and Asia, because anyone who looked soft on communism risked a political attack.
points: Republicans charged from late 1949 that Truman and the State Department had lost China, after the communist victory. McCarthy's attacks on State Department officials amplified the charge.

Owen Lattimore, a Johns Hopkins China scholar, was accused by McCarthy in March 1950 of being a leading Soviet agent. He was never charged with espionage; he was indicted for perjury in 1952, and the charges were dropped in 1955.

State Department China specialists John Paton Davies and John S. Service were removed from their posts: Service was dismissed in 1951 and Davies in 1954. This weakened the government's expert knowledge of Asia.
The campaign made it politically risky for Democrats to show any willingness to negotiate with communist states, which constrained diplomacy in the Korean and Chinese crises.

John Foster Dulles was secretary of state from 1953 to 1959, and his department, with security chief Scott McLeod, applied the new security standards. The climate pressed the administration to avoid any open conflict with McCarthy.

Soviet propaganda and allied critics used McCarthyism, and images of racial violence and discrimination such as the Little Rock crisis of 1957, to argue that American democracy was a sham, which damaged America's image abroad.
notes.tip: Link McCarthy to foreign policy through China and Asia: the loss of China charge, the purge of experts such as Lattimore, Davies and Service, and the political cost of negotiating with communists. That link earns more credit than narrating his career.

notes.h: The anti-war movement begins: teach-ins, SDS and the draft
notes.b: Opposition to the Vietnam War started on university campuses in 1965 and grew into a mass movement. Students had a personal stake because the draft could send them to fight.
points: The first major teach-in (an all-night meeting of lectures and debate) was held at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, on 24 and 25 March 1965. Several thousand attended, and teach-ins spread to many campuses in the following weeks.

Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) emerged in 1960 and was famous for the Port Huron Statement of 1962, largely written by Tom Hayden. Its Washington march of April 1965 drew about 15,000 to 25,000 people.
By 1969 SDS had split, with the Weathermen emerging from it. This fragmentation shows that the movement was divided as well as large.
The Selective Service System (the draft) called up men aged 18 to 26. Student deferments favoured the better-off, so poorer and Black men were more likely to be sent to Vietnam.

Many young men resisted by burning draft cards or going to Canada. The first draft lottery, which selected men for call-up by birthdate, was held on 1 December 1969 and made young men more aware of the war's impact on their lives.
Muhammad Ali, formerly Cassius Clay, refused induction in Houston on 28 April 1967, citing his religious beliefs as a Nation of Islam minister. He was stripped of the world title and boxing licence.

He was convicted of draft evasion in June 1967 (five years and a fine; he stayed free on appeal), and the Supreme Court overturned the conviction in June 1971. As a famous champion, his refusal made the draft a matter of conscience for a mass audience.
notes.tip: Examiners credit naming where the movement began (campuses, the 1965 teach-ins), who led it (SDS) and how the draft fed it. Keep Ali's refusal of April 1967 separate from the Supreme Court ruling of 1971.

notes.h: The anti-war movement at its height, 1967 to 1969
notes.b: From 1967 protest moved from the campuses into churches, the streets and the national conventions. Television brought each event to a mass audience, which made it hard for the government to ignore.
points: On 4 April 1967, at Riverside Church in New York, Martin Luther King gave his 'Beyond Vietnam' speech. He called the US government 'the greatest purveyor of violence in the world today', and argued that the war drained resources from the war on poverty.
King was criticised by some allies and by the press for linking civil rights to the war, but his speech made opposition to Vietnam part of the Black freedom struggle.

The March on the Pentagon on 21 October 1967 drew tens of thousands and many arrests. Norman Mailer took part and wrote The Armies of the Night (1968), which won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award.

The Democratic National Convention met in Chicago from 26 to 29 August 1968. Police and the National Guard clashed with protesters in Grant Park and on Michigan Avenue, under Mayor Richard Daley, in front of television cameras.
The protesters chanted that the whole world was watching, because the violence was being broadcast live. Hubert Humphrey was nominated.
The Vietnam Moratorium of 15 October 1969 brought demonstrations across the country. A separate large march followed in Washington on 15 November 1969, and it must not be called a Moratorium.
Nixon replied with a televised speech on 3 November 1969, appealing to the silent majority of Americans who did not protest. This shows that many Americans disapproved of the protesters.
notes.tip: Examiners credit Ali's refusal and King's 1967 speech as separate strands. Say that only 15 October 1969 was the Moratorium; the November march was a separate mobilisation. Put the Pentagon march (1967, protest) apart from the Pentagon Papers (1971, leaked study).

notes.h: Cambodia, Kent State, the Pentagon Papers and the effect on policy
notes.b: In 1970 and 1971 anger over the widening war led to deaths on campuses and a leak that damaged the government's case. Together they pressed Nixon to bring troops home.
points: Nixon announced the Cambodian incursion on 30 April 1970, and campus protests and a student strike followed. This is why the war's widening, not only its length, sparked protest.

On 4 May 1970 Ohio National Guardsmen fired on students at Kent State University, killing four and wounding nine. At Jackson State in Mississippi, on 15 May 1970, police killed two. Kent State was in Ohio and Jackson State in Mississippi.

The Pentagon Papers were a secret Defense Department history of US involvement in Vietnam, leaked by Daniel Ellsberg. The New York Times began publishing on 13 June 1971, the government obtained a halt, and the Supreme Court ruled for the press on 30 June 1971.

Congress repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, the August 1964 vote that had given the president wide war powers, in January 1971, and in 1973 it cut off funds for US combat in Indochina, so Congress itself began to act against the war.

Protest and public opinion put pressure on Nixon to withdraw troops and to Vietnamise the war (hand more fighting to South Vietnamese forces). Johnson's decision of March 1968 not to seek re-election was also a response to public opinion.
notes.tip: Place events by date and state: Kent State (4 May 1970, Ohio, National Guard), Jackson State (15 May 1970, Mississippi) and Chicago 1968 are often confused. Kent State did not cause the Cooper-Church amendment; the Cambodian incursion did.

notes.h: Race relations and the Cold War image of the United States
notes.b: Racial discrimination at home was a serious problem for US foreign policy, because it weakened America's claim to lead the free world. The audience that mattered was the newly independent states of Asia and Africa.
points: President Truman's Executive Order 9981, of 26 July 1948, ordered equality of treatment in the armed services. It was partly motivated by the need to answer communist criticism of US racism; Truman also faced the 1948 election and the Black vote. Full integration took years, until the Korean War.

In Brown v. Board of Education, on 17 May 1954, the Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional. The ruling was reported abroad as evidence of progress, though desegregation was slow in the South.
The Justice Department's brief in Brown urged the Court to remember the effect abroad, since segregation was a Cold War embarrassment, a point Mary Dudziak later stressed.

At Little Rock Central High School in September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus resisted the entry of nine Black students. Eisenhower sent federal troops (the 101st Airborne) to enforce it, and Soviet media used the images around the world.

The Freedom Rides of May 1961 (buses attacked in Alabama) and the Birmingham campaign of spring 1963 (police dogs and fire hoses used on children, widely televised) were international news. They undermined the US claim to be a model of democracy.

Soviet and Chinese propaganda broadcast stories of segregation and racial violence to the Third World, which is why US diplomats argued that events like Little Rock damaged the country's standing in newly independent Asian and African states.

Black leaders linked race to foreign policy. King tied the cost of the war in Vietnam to the funds needed for the poor. Malcolm X toured Africa in 1964 and argued that the American struggle was an international human rights matter.

The Civil Rights Act of July 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of August 1965 were landmark reforms. Historians such as Mary Dudziak (Cold War Civil Rights, 2000) argue that foreign opinion was one factor, though not the main one.
notes.tip: A paragraph on Little Rock or Brown earns credit when linked to foreign policy through the Soviet response, rather than just narrated. Do not claim that Cold War credibility was the stated purpose of the 1964 or 1965 laws.

notes.h: Assessment: how far did domestic pressures shape foreign policy?
notes.b: Judgements that weigh the pressure of domestic fears, protest and race against the Cold War and strategic aims earn the most credit. Each force had real effects and clear limits.
points: McCarthyism was the strongest constraint in the early 1950s: it damaged civil liberties, weakened expert advice on China and Asia, and made negotiation with communists risky. But the Red Scare predated McCarthy and outlasted him, and some Soviet spying was real, as the Venona decrypts show.

The anti-war movement shaped public opinion, Johnson's decision of 1968 and the pace of Nixon's withdrawals. But it was divided, often unpopular with the silent majority, and the war continued for four more years after Johnson's decision.
Historians disagree about whether protests changed the outcome of the war or simply sharpened a decision the government had already reached.

Race relations were an embarrassment that pushed leaders towards reform, because Soviet propaganda used Little Rock and Birmingham. But reform was driven mainly by the Black freedom movement itself and by domestic politics.
Overall, domestic opinion limited and shaped policy, but strategic and Cold War considerations stayed the main drivers of US foreign policy.

Contemporaries often saw McCarthy and the protesters through party and class lines. Later historians such as Rovere and Schrecker judge McCarthyism harshly, while Evans defends it using Venona, so the verdict depends on the view taken.
notes.tip: The 100-mark essay is usually a comparison. Open with the judgement: McCarthyism narrowed choices on China and Asia in the early 1950s, while the anti-war movement worked later through public opinion on Johnson in 1968 and Nixon after. Give dated evidence for each.

keyTerms.definition: The views of ordinary Americans, measured by polls and reported by the press, which shaped the limits of foreign policy and the fate of the Vietnam War.
Newspapers, radio and television, which in this period carried the McCarthy hearings, the Vietnam war reports and the protests to national audiences.
A tradition in US politics supporting civil liberties, civil rights and an active federal government, which was attacked by McCarthy and defended by the anti-war and civil rights movements.
The practice of making reckless accusations of communist subversion against officials and private citizens, named after Senator Joseph McCarthy.
The wave of fear of communist subversion in the United States from the late 1940s to the mid-1950s, which led to blacklists and loyalty checks.
A public meeting held on a campus in which faculty and students debated the Vietnam War, the first major one being at the University of Michigan in March 1965.
The televised Senate hearings of April to June 1954 into McCarthy's charges against the army, which damaged his public standing.
The secret government study of US involvement in Vietnam, published by the New York Times in June 1971.
Ten film writers and directors who refused to answer HUAC's questions about communism in 1947, were convicted of contempt of Congress and were blacklisted by the studios.
The House Un-American Activities Committee, which investigated alleged communist influence in the film industry and government from the late 1940s.
